notes: First sourced rules for the Northern Territory, territory-wide. references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Development applications are decided by the Development Consent Authority within its division areas and by the Minister outside them, and are administered by Development Assessment Services. You may need a development permit to build something new, extend your home, change a use or subdivide. Lodge through Development Applications Online with contact details, owner's authorisation if needed, a statement of effect addressing section 46 of the Planning Act 1999, dimensioned plans and an image. Processing takes approximately 8 weeks. Exhibition, when required, is 7, 14 or 28 days. All fees are non-refundable. You can apply to the NT Civil and Administrative Tribunal for a review within 28 days.
references.interpretation: The NT Government, not councils, decides development applications. Timeframes and exhibition periods to quote. Captured on 2026-10-12 from an automated summary of the published page; the exact wording was not available. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Permitted uses need no development permit if they meet all relevant development, subdivision and consolidation requirements and no overlay applies; a building permit may still be needed in a building control area and the certifier must be satisfied about planning compliance. A permitted use becomes merit assessable if an overlay requires consent or a requirement is varied. Merit assessable uses need a development permit and are likely to be approved if they meet the requirements. Impact assessable uses need a development permit and may be refused even if they meet the requirements. Prohibited uses can only get a permit in limited cases.

references.section: Development permit, advertising and variation fees
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Development permit fees: use with no physical development $290; single dwelling on one lot $269; estimated cost $100,000 or less $269; over $100,000 to $250,000 $810; over $250,000 to $1 million $1,175; over $1 million to $10 million $4,172; subdivision, consolidation or boundary realignment $1,162 plus $56 per lot. Advertising $149 per exhibition period. Certificate of compliance for subdivision $0, other development $254. Variation of a development permit $223 or 10% of the application fee. Extension 50% of the application fee. Compliance check $402 or 20% of the fee. All fees non-refundable.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Amendment 94 (from 1 December 2023) increased the maximum floor area for independent units to 75 square metres in certain zones. No development permit is needed where the use is permitted, no overlays apply and all requirements are met; otherwise a development permit is needed. Building approval from an NT registered building certifier is needed, and occupancy certification (or a builder's declaration in a tier 2 building control area) before occupying. Planning approval must come before occupancy certification. A separate title through a unit title scheme subdivision is not allowed; a freehold subdivision only if it meets all subdivision requirements including minimum lot size.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The NT Planning Scheme has land subject to flooding and land subject to storm surge overlays. Storm surge inundation maps and floodplain maps are published. No bushfire overlay is mentioned.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] You must engage a registered private building certifier for most building projects. The certifier assesses plans and issues the building permit, then lodges it with the Director of Building Control. Without occupancy certification you can't legally occupy the building.

references.section: Heritage properties: building works and development
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Work on a heritage place is regulated under the Heritage Act 2011. Exempt work (defined in the Heritage Regulations 2012) needs no formal approval. Minor works are decided by the Heritage Council and major works by the Minister for Lands, Planning and Environment. Heritage NT decides which category applies. Discuss the work with Heritage NT first, then submit the application to carry out work on a heritage place or object. You are told of the decision in writing. Contact: Heritage Branch, 08 8999 5039, heritage.branch@nt.gov.au. No fees or timeframes are stated.
references.interpretation: Work on a declared heritage place needs heritage approval unless exempt, separate from any development permit. rules.title: A development permit may be needed, depending on zone and overlays

outcomes.title: You may need a development permit
outcomes.detail: In the NT, the NT Government's Development Consent Authority decides development applications, not your council. Under the NT Planning Scheme 2020, a permitted use (like a house in many residential zones) needs no development permit if it meets every requirement and no overlay applies. If you need to vary a requirement, an overlay applies, or the use is merit or impact assessable, you need a development permit. It takes about 8 weeks. The fee for a single dwelling on one lot is $269. Check your zone and overlays on the NT Atlas.

rules.title: Building work needs a building permit in building control areas

outcomes.title: You likely need a building permit from a registered building certifier
outcomes.detail: In the NT's building control areas (including Darwin, Alice Springs, Katherine and Tennant Creek), you need a building permit before you start. You get it from a registered private building certifier, not the council. The certifier checks your plans against the National Construction Code and needs any development permit first. A permit lasts two years.

approval.pathway: Building permit under the Building Act 1993 (National Construction Code)

evidence.title: Structural engineer's certification of the design
Site plan, floor plans and elevations to scale

payload.task: Engage an NT registered building certifier

rules.notes: LIKELY_REQUIRED: most NT towns are building control areas; land outside them may not need a permit.

rules.title: Occupancy certification before you move in

outcomes.title: You likely need occupancy certification before you move in
outcomes.detail: When the work is finished, apply to your building certifier for occupancy certification, usually an occupancy permit. You can't legally occupy the building without it. In tier 2 building control areas (like Katherine and Tennant Creek), a house can be part certified, and you get a builder's declaration instead.

approval.pathway: Occupancy certification (occupancy permit) under the Building Act 1993

payload.task: Ask your certifier which inspections and documents you need for occupancy

rules.title: Heritage places need heritage works approval

outcomes.title: Heritage listing means you likely need heritage works approval
outcomes.detail: If your property is a declared heritage place on the NT Heritage Register, work on it needs approval under the Heritage Act 2011 unless it is exempt. Heritage NT decides whether your work is exempt, minor (decided by the Heritage Council) or major (decided by the Minister). Talk to the Heritage Branch on 08 8999 5039 before you design, then apply. You may also need a development permit and a building permit.

approval.authority: Heritage Council (minor works) or the Minister (major works), through Heritage NT
approval.pathway: Approval to carry out work on a heritage place under the Heritage Act 2011

evidence.title: Description of the work and its effect on the heritage place

payload.task: Search the NT Heritage Register and call Heritage NT

rules.notes: LIKELY_REQUIRED: the user ticked heritage, but exempt work needs no approval.

rules.title: Flood and storm surge overlays need a development permit

outcomes.title: Flooding or storm surge means you likely need a development permit
outcomes.detail: The NT Planning Scheme 2020 has land subject to flooding and land subject to storm surge overlays. You need planning approval to develop zoned land at risk from riverine flooding or storm surge, even for a use that would otherwise be permitted. Check the storm surge and floodplain maps, and the overlays on the NT Atlas.

rules.title: Independent units up to 75 m2

outcomes.title: At 75 m2 or less, your independent unit fits the NT size limit
outcomes.detail: Since 1 December 2023 (Amendment 94), the NT Planning Scheme 2020 allows independent units up to 75 m2 in certain zones. If the use is permitted in your zone, no overlay applies and you meet every requirement, you don't need a development permit. You still need a building permit and occupancy certification.

payload.task: Check your zone's assessment table in Part 4 of the NT Planning Scheme 2020

outcomes.title: Over 75 m2, your independent unit likely needs a development permit or a redesign
outcomes.detail: Independent units over 75 m2 exceed the NT Planning Scheme 2020 limit. You would need a development permit to vary the requirement, or it may be treated as a second dwelling, which may not be allowed in your zone.

outcomes.detail: You need a development permit if an independent unit is merit or impact assessable in your zone, if an overlay applies, or if you want to vary a requirement such as setbacks, height or parking.

outcomes.title: You can't put an independent unit on its own unit title
outcomes.detail: In the NT you can't create a separate title for an independent unit through a unit title scheme. A separate freehold lot is only possible if the subdivision meets every requirement of the NT Planning Scheme 2020, including minimum lot size.

outcomes.title: You need a development permit to subdivide, then survey approval and new titles
outcomes.detail: To subdivide in the NT you need a development permit from the Development Consent Authority ($1,162 plus $56 per lot). Then a licensed surveyor gets lot numbers and addresses, you complete the works, get a certificate of compliance, get Land Titles Office concurrence and Surveyor-General approval of the plan, and lodge for new titles. Rural and unzoned land also needs a land suitability assessment.

rules.title: New titles from the Land Titles Office

outcomes.title: New titles come after the Surveyor-General approves the plan
outcomes.detail: Once the plan is approved, you pay the fee and lodge with the Land Titles Office: the approved survey plan, consents and the NT Land Titles Office application for separate titles (form 21). Titles can be issued within 24 business hours. Paper titles are no longer issued.

outcomes.detail: In the NT, development applications go to the Development Consent Authority through Development Applications Online.
